Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
Nothing good can happen to me anymore

vignette: Rohan's eyes still widen when he recalls the chill of the handcuffs on his wrists, the metallic taste in his mouth as he lay on the pavement. It was a sweltering summer evening two years ago, and Rohan, then 24, had been stopped by police for a routine traffic check. The situation escalated quickly; he remembers feeling disoriented, unable to process what was happening. A female officer stood over him, her voice firm but detached, as she explained that he fit the description of a suspect in a nearby robbery. The memory of that night still makes Rohan's skin crawl, and not just because of the physical discomfort. It's the sense of helplessness, of being at the mercy of strangers who didn't seem to care about his innocence. When he thinks back, he's overcome with grief, as if reliving the event all over again. Sometimes, he catches a whiff of something - exhaust fumes, sweat, and ozone - and it transports him right back to that pavement. In the months following the incident, Rohan started to notice strange physical sensations when memories of that night resurfaced. His body would contort into the same position as when he was pinned down by the officers - his shoulders tense, his legs twisted at an awkward angle. It's as if his body is trying to recreate the trauma, reenacting it in painful detail. Rohan has become increasingly withdrawn, avoiding situations that remind him of that night. He's developed a strange aversion to being alone with women, even his wife, Nalini. She tries to be understanding, but Rohan can sense her frustration. It's not just the physical distance; he feels emotionally detached from her, as if he's watching their interactions through a haze. Even simple tasks have become daunting challenges. As an editor, Rohan works with writers of all backgrounds, but now he finds himself avoiding female contributors or, worse still, making excuses to work remotely when they come into the office. His relationships with colleagues are strained; they notice his detachment and assume it's just a phase. Rohan is tormented by thoughts that he's not coping well enough. He's always prided himself on being resilient, but this experience has shaken him to the core. He's lost interest in activities he once loved - reading, hiking, cooking - and now feels like nothing brings meaning to his life. It's as if the world has turned against him; every encounter with authority figures or women fills him with dread. Lately, Rohan's begun to wonder if anything good can happen to him again. He feels stuck in a never-ending cycle of fear and anxiety, unsure how to break free. Nalini has encouraged him to seek help, but he's hesitant - what if talking about this makes it worse? What if he's not strong enough to confront the demons that haunt him? As Rohan sits on his couch, staring blankly at the wall, he knows something needs to change. He can't keep living like this, trapped in a world of triggers and avoidance behaviors. The thought sends a shiver down his spine - is it possible for him to find peace again?
